Transition to larger size scales and comparison with industrial scale One-carbon (C1) compounds are increasingly recognized as cost-effective and potentially carbon-negative feedstocks for biomanufacturing. These compounds provide the basis for efficient and versatile metabolic platforms capable of synthesizing a variety of value-added products. The Synthetic formyl-CoA elongation (FORCE) pathways facilitate the synthesis of diverse products from C1 compounds through iterative C1 elongation, operating independently from the host metabolism. This reduces engineering complexity and potentially enhances theoretical yields. However, the kinetics of the core C1–C1 condensation enzyme, 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA synthase (HACS), which catalyzes the acyloin condensation reaction between formaldehyde and formyl- CoA, has been a significant bottleneck. Addressing this, we utilized a combinatorial approach of bioprospecting and rational protein engineering to identify and enhance multiple HACS variants. These efforts significantly improved their activity toward C1 substrates. Through sequence and structure alignment, key regions essential for catalytic function were identified and targeted for mutagenesis, resulting in enhanced catalytic efficiency. Concurrently, additional rounds of bioprospecting were conducted to identify homologs with high sequence similarity to active variants, aiming to discover HACS variants with even higher activity. Biological Upconversion Ethylene glycol, a critical bulk chemical used in biodegradable plastics like polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and as a component in antifreeze agents and coolants, presents a prime target for sustainable production methods. Traditional synthetic routes for ethylene glycol rely on fossil resources and are marked by high energy consumption. Biotechnological advances offer alternative biosynthetic pathways, primarily through fermentation and whole-cell transformation. These traditionally use sugars like xylose, glucose, cellulose, and arabinose in engineered bacteria such as E. coli and yeast. 16 Notable studies have highlighted these methods, though they suffer from significant drawbacks, including the difficulty of separating by-products and low conversion rates due to the complex multi-step nature of the pathways (Salusjärvi, L. et al., 2019). More recent innovations have explored enzymatic cascades, such as those utilizing GALD synthase (GALS) to catalyze formaldehyde into ethylene glycol (Zhou, J. et al., 2022). However, while precise, these in vitro enzyme-based methods struggle with scalability and fail to replicate the intricate metabolic interactions present in living cells. As such, there is an ongoing need to develop alternative routes that utilize economically viable bulk chemicals to convert to ethylene glycol, aiming to overcome these limitations and enhance the feasibility of sustainable large-scale production.
